title: Redis Client Configuration Best Practices
description: Configure ioredis correctly for development, staging, and production to avoid connection failures and data loss.

data.text: A Redis client is only as reliable as its configuration. Incorrect timeouts, missing retry strategies, and weak connection pools cause cascading failures in production. This lesson covers the essential settings every Node.js service should apply to its ioredis instance.

The ioredis constructor accepts host, port, password, and database as first-class options. Beyond those, `connectTimeout` and `lazyConnect` are the two settings most likely to prevent startup crashes. A sensible retry strategy with a maximum backoff cap prevents thundering-herd reconnections.

rows: true for serverless, false for long-running

data.text: The following configuration balances resilience and speed. The retry strategy caps at 2 seconds so a failing Redis does not hold open connections indefinitely. keepAlive sends TCP probes to detect silently dropped connections.

data.title: Production-ready Redis configuration
data.content: Apply these settings in every environment above local development.

data.text: Every Redis command can take an optional timeout in milliseconds. Without one, a slow Redis instance can hold a request open indefinitely. Apply timeouts to SET, GET, and pipeline calls in your caching layer.

data.title: Applying per-command timeouts
data.content: Wrap SET and GET with explicit 100 ms timeouts.

data.title: Never Skip Timeouts in Production
data.text: A Redis command with no timeout can hang a request handler, exhaust the event loop, and take down your service. Always set a command-level or global socket timeout.

Local development usually uses a local Redis at port 6379 with no password. Staging and production use managed Redis (ElastiCache, Memorystore, Upstash) with authentication, TLS, and connection limits. Keep credentials in environment variables — never hardcode them.

data.title: Environment configuration rules
items: local: lazyConnect false, no retry cap, enableOfflineQueue true
staging: same options as production but with staging host and retry cap 5
production: lazyConnect true, retry cap 3, keepAlive true, maxRetriesPerRequest 3
Always load host, port, password from process.env
Use a separate Redis database number per environment (db: 0 vs 1)

data.caption: Environment-specific Redis client configuration

items.text: REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_PASSWORD loaded from environment variables
connectTimeout set to 5000 ms or lower
retryStrategy configured with a maximum backoff cap
keepAlive enabled for long-running Node.js processes
maxRetriesPerRequest set to 3 for production writes
Per-command timeouts added to caching helper functions

items.question: Should I use TLS for Redis?
items.answer: Yes, in managed cloud environments (ElastiCache with in-transit encryption, Upstash, Redis Enterprise). ioredis supports TLS via the tls option in the constructor.

items.question: What is enableOfflineQueue?
items.answer: When true, ioredis buffers commands during disconnection and replays them on reconnect. Disable it in production to avoid sending stale commands after a failover.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Set connectTimeout to 5 seconds and always apply per-command timeouts.
Use lazyConnect and maxRetriesPerRequest in production only.
Keep keepAlive enabled to detect dead TCP connections early.
Load all connection settings from environment variables.
